payload.rationale: Global temperatures are on a steady upward trend due to climate change, making new annual temperature records relatively frequent. However, year-to-year variability, largely driven by the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), means that not every year sets a new record. Without specific data for the 2025 baseline value or the temperature anomalies for the first eight months of 2026, we must rely on historical base rates. In recent decades, new global temperature records have occurred approximately every 3 to 4 years, suggesting a baseline probability of around 25-35% for any specific future year. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is if 2025 set an exceptionally high record (making it very difficult for 2026 to exceed it) or if 2026 coincides with a strong La Niña phase, which typically depresses global average temperatures. The strongest reason this estimate could be too low is if 2026 experiences a strong El Niño event or if underlying warming trends accelerate faster than anticipated, making a new record highly likely.
limitations: Lack of data regarding the 2025 NASA GISS temperature anomaly.
No information on the ENSO state or temperature anomalies for the first eight months of 2026.
